stages.name: Profit vs not-for-profit
stages.title: Profit vs not-for-profit
stages.sub: How to tell apart businesses that exist to make money and organisations that exist to serve a cause.

steps.q: A café sells coffee for £3 that cost £1 to make. What do we call the £3 it takes in from selling?
steps.right: The total money it takes in
steps.wrong: The money left over after costs
steps.hint: Is this the whole amount coming in, or only what remains after costs?
steps.pre: The money a sale brings in is called

steps.q: A gym owner sets prices to leave as much money as possible left over after costs, and pays this leftover to herself. What kind of business is this?
steps.right: One set up to make money for its owner
steps.wrong: One set up to fund a cause
steps.hint: Who benefits from the money left over after costs here?

steps.q: A charity shop sells donated clothes. Its founders set it up so that any leftover money goes towards housing homeless people, not to themselves. What kind of organisation is this?
steps.right: One set up to serve a social aim, not to enrich its owners
steps.wrong: One set up to make money for its owner
steps.hint: Who is meant to gain from the money left over after costs here?

steps.q: Both the gym and the charity shop end the month with money left over after costs. Where does that leftover money go in each case?
steps.right: To the owner in one, the cause in the other
steps.wrong: To the owner in both of the cases
steps.hint: Think about who actually keeps the surplus once costs are paid in each case.

steps.prompt: Drag and drop the 4 key terms in the order they build on each other.

steps.q: Using what happens to the leftover money as the test, are the gym and the charity shop the same type of organisation or different types?
steps.hint: One keeps the surplus for its owner, the other feeds it back into a cause. Does that make them alike or unlike?
